entities.name: Lançarote de Freitas
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lançarote de Freitas, a prominent 15th-century Portuguese navigator and slave trader, emerged from Lagos, Portugal, to become a central figure in the nascent European transatlantic slave trade. Operating under the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator, his expeditions between 1444 and 1446 marked a critical escalation in the systematic capture and transportation of West Africans to Portugal, profoundly shaping the economic and moral trajectory of the Age of Discovery. His actions transformed incidental raiding into an organized, profitable enterprise, setting a brutal precedent for future colonial exploitation.

In 1444, Lançarote commanded a fleet of six caravels, sailing from Lagos to the Bay of Arguin (modern-day Mauritania), where his forces launched a brutal surprise attack on a local fishing village, capturing 235 individuals. These captives were then brought back to Lagos, where they were publicly paraded and divided, with a fifth reserved for Prince Henry. A second, equally devastating expedition in 1445-1446, involving fourteen vessels, further solidified the profitability and tactical blueprint of these raids, extending Portuguese reach along the Senegambian coast and capturing hundreds more, despite encountering increased resistance from local populations.

Lançarote de Freitas's expeditions were instrumental in establishing the economic viability and operational model for the Portuguese slave trade, directly influencing the development of large-scale chattel slavery in the Atlantic world. His success provided crucial funding and impetus for subsequent Portuguese explorations and colonial ventures along the African coast, legitimizing the horrific practice of human trafficking as a cornerstone of imperial expansion. The wealth generated from these early slave raids fueled further maritime innovation and territorial claims, embedding the institution of slavery deep within the fabric of European colonial ambition.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lançarote de Freitas was a pivotal figure in the early establishment of the direct European maritime slave trade, initiating systematic raids that brought hundreds of West Africans to Portugal. His expeditions laid the operational and economic groundwork for the transatlantic slave trade, profoundly shaping the trajectory of European colonial expansion and the suffering of millions.

entities.summary:
Lançarote de Freitas, often identified as Lançarote de Lagos or da Ilha, stands as a pivotal yet morally complex figure in the early history of European maritime expansion, particularly recognized for his role in initiating the large-scale, direct sea-based slave trade from West Africa to Portugal. A 15th-century Portuguese explorer and merchant from Lagos, he leveraged the evolving navigational technologies and the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator to launch expeditions that dramatically altered the trajectory of both European economic development and African demography. His voyages in the mid-1440s mark a grim turning point, transitioning from sporadic capture to systematic, commercially driven human trafficking.

His notoriety stems primarily from two major expeditions between 1444 and 1446. In 1444, leading a fleet of six caravels from Lagos, Lançarote targeted the coastal regions near Arguin Bay (modern-day Mauritania), capturing approximately 235 individuals, primarily from the Azenegue (Berber) and Wolof peoples. This mass enslavement culminated in a chilling public auction in Lagos, meticulously documented by Gomes Eanes de Zurara, which served to normalize and legitimize the burgeoning slave trade in Portugal. A subsequent expedition in 1445, also under his command, continued this brutal pattern, further entrenching the economic viability of human exploitation as a core component of Portuguese overseas ventures.
